newsitem.title: USA: Thurmond carves another longevity notch.
newsitem.headline: Thurmond carves another longevity notch.

text.p: At age 94, Strom Thurmond on Sunday carved another notch in his longevity belt, becoming the longest-serving senator in the history of the United States.
Indeed, the courtly South Carolinian's 42-year tenure represents one-fifth of the Senate's own 208-year history.

Despite his slowing pace, the conservative Republican was easily re-elected to an eighth term in November 1996. He beat a Democrat less than half his age who was born the year Thurmond won election as a write-in candidate in 1954.

Thurmond says he plans to finish out this term, taking him to January 2003. That means if his recipe for longevity -- fresh fruit, daily exercise and "an optimistic attitude toward life" -- holds, he could celebrate his 100th birthday under the Capitol dome Dec. 5, 2002.

Already the oldest man ever to serve as senator, he now surpasses the length of service record set by Arizona Democrat Carl Hayden on Jan. 2, 1969. He died after holding office 41 years and 10 months.
Thurmond plans on marking the milestone Sunday with a speech in Johnston, South Carolina, in Edgefield County, where he was born in 1902.

Overall, he said, life in the Senate has not changed very much in 40 years. Senators, he said, are no better or worse than they used to be. The one difference, he said, is "in the last 30 years, they have been spending more."

Thurmond, who has been a Democrat, a "Dixiecrat" and a Republican but always a conservative, told reporters last week that his priorities on the first day on the job were to get "sworn in and find where the payroll office was."

Later, he turned his attention to defence and veterans' affairs and is now chairman of the Armed Services Committee. In a floor speech Friday before heading home for Memorial Day, he extolled the importance of military cemeteries and said he was introducing a bill to protect against vandalism of soldiers' graves.
After the week-long recess, his colleagues plan on offering tributes to him in the Senate.
His former Senate colleague, Bob Dole, called Thurmond "an American original, an inspiration to millions, and one of the most enduring figures in American political history."

Dole, who made an unsuccessful bid to become the oldest newly elected president at age 73, in a statement said: "May he extend his record as long as he wishes, and knowing Strom, he's got another 41 years of service in him -- at least."

A staunch segregationist who ran for president in 1948 on a third-party "Dixiecrat" ticket, Thurmond's political career got its start in the Southern white struggle against civil rights. He still holds the record for controlling the Senate floor longer than anyone else. In 1957 he spoke nonstop against a civil rights bill for 24 hours and 18 minutes.
But he had to accommodate to the changing nature of race relations, as well as to the new role of women. But he said he rather enjoys having women colleagues.
"They are smart and we like to look at them," he quipped.
